title: Deity yoga, explained
hookLine: visualizing oneself as an awakened figure, understood as empty and luminous

lines: THE PICTURE YOU CARRY OF YOURSELF.
cards: What comes up when you picture yourself? For some people it's someone a little tired, a little behind, with a list of flaws ready to recite.
A picture like that can run all day, mostly unnoticed, shaping what seems possible. Tibetan tantric Buddhism does something bold with that habit. It doesn't argue with the old picture.
It replaces it, on purpose, for the length of a meditation, with the picture of an awakened being. To an outsider it can look like pretending. Today, what it actually is.

teach.b: In Vajrayana, the diamond vehicle you met in year one, the practitioner visualizes themselves as an awakened figure, such as Tara or Avalokiteshvara, with a body made of light and the surroundings as a pure land.
The deity isn't a god to be pleased from a distance. It's a form of awakening itself. Second, empty and luminous.
The practice usually begins by letting the ordinary self-image dissolve into emptiness.

teach.h: ARISING FROM EMPTINESS, LIKE A RAINBOW.
teach.b: Then the deity arises out of it, clear and vivid, but without solid substance, like a rainbow or a reflection in a mirror. Teachers call that the guardrail.
If the figure were solid, they say, this would just be a fancier ego. Because it's understood as empty, it loosens the grip of every self-image, the old one included.
Third, two qualities Tibetan teachers name: clear appearance, seeing the form vividly, and what's often called divine pride, a steady confidence of being awakened that isn't the ego's pride at all.

teach.h: LEARNED WITH EMPOWERMENT AND A TEACHER.
teach.b: In Tibetan traditions, full deity yoga is practiced after receiving empowerment and instruction from a qualified teacher, usually on top of the foundations you met this week.
So this is an explanation, not the practice.

Each of this week's steps, one intention, all the way down, the foundations, the whole world offered, washed clean, joining minds, clears ground, so that seeing yourself as awakened rests on something real.

how: Tibetan Buddhist practitioners take up deity yoga after receiving empowerment and instruction from a teacher, typically meditating daily with a practice text in which they arise as the deity from emptiness and recite the deity's mantra.

o: seeing yourself as an awakened figure, empty and bright
imagining yourself as a perfect version of your ego
worshiping a god from a distance to win its favor

p: like a rainbow or a reflection

s: in deity yoga the figure is a god to be pleased from a distance
the practitioner arises as the figure, understood as a form of awakening itself.
the deity is visualized as solid and real like a statue
it arises from emptiness, vivid but without solid substance, like a rainbow.
in Tibetan traditions, full deity yoga follows empowerment and instruction
today's lesson is an explanation, not the practice itself.

games.q: you've read about deity yoga and want to start the full practice tonight, from a book. what do Tibetan traditions say comes first?
o: empowerment and instruction from a qualified teacher.
games.why: full deity yoga is practiced after empowerment and instruction, usually on the foundations of this week's lessons.

practice: This isn't deity yoga, just a small taste of the idea, open to anyone: let your usual picture of yourself soften, the list and the flaws, like mist thinning.
Then picture yourself made of kindness, clear as a reflection, with nothing solid to defend, and feel how that body would sit and breathe. When the old picture returns, let it pass like weather.

wordCard.voice: Deity yoga. Seeing yourself as an awakened figure, understood as empty and luminous, like a rainbow. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit devata: deity. Tibetan Buddhists use yidam for the deity a practitioner meditates on.

carryVoice: Your line: as the deity. Clear as a rainbow, with nothing solid to defend. Rest well.
